newsitem.title: USA: Color blind blood test may help children.
newsitem.headline: Color blind blood test may help children.

text.p: A simple new experimental blood test can detect colour blindness and measure its severity, researchers said on Thursday.
A test could help determine if a child is learning-disabled, or is merely having trouble with colour-coded basic learning tools.

"When my brother-in-law was a child, he was labeld as 'not being able to follow directions.' But he was colour-blind -- when they told him to colour the clown's nose red, he was at a loss," said Jay Neitz, who developed the test with his wife and colleague Maureen Neitz at the Eye Institute of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee.

A simple colour blindness test may also become valuable in evaluating colour vision for job skills ranging from jet fighter pilots to pharmaceutical inspectors to many professions that rely more and more on colour-coded computer information, he said.

The test, described in Friday's edition of the journal Science, is still experimental and there are not yet firm plans on how to commercialize it, although Jay Neitz said in a telephone interview, "We want to do something that has practical interest ... I hope we can bring it to the public."

He said the blood test techniques they have developed may someday also prove useful in evaluating other more complex genetic disorders that affect behaviour, possibly including mental illnesses with a genetic component.

"The only way you know (people have these problems) is that they act differently. They don't have a tumour, there's nothing you can cut open," he said. "Actions are the only way you can identify what's different, because what's different is in their central nervous system."
About one-in-10 men have some degree of colour blindness, and about one-in-20 have a form of red-green colour blindness known as deuteranomaly.

In a Science article last year, the Neitzs showed there were at least 10 pigment genes in colourblindness. That overturned 200 years of conventional wisdom that there were three genes, for each of the primary colours, red, green and blue.
